title: Chidi and the Thirteenth Hour
blurb: A brass clock with thirteen numbers gives Chidi an extra hour every day. But every hour has an owner.

chapters.title: The Clock with Thirteen Numbers
chapters.text:
Chidi never had enough time. His school day in Lagos began at seven, football practice ended at five, and then came homework, chores and his little sister Ngozi, who needed help with her violin. By bedtime, Chidi was always behind. There was always one more page, one more plate to wash, one more scale for Ngozi that he promised to hear tomorrow.

Their mother worked long shifts at the hospital, and their father drove a delivery van to Ibadan three days a week. So the two children looked after each other more than most. Ngozi was eight, and she played the violin as if she were telling it a secret. Chidi was twelve, and his homework diary was full of red ink. It said late, and late again, and once, in his teacher's tired handwriting, simply, oh, Chidi.

One Saturday, he wandered into the repair shop at the end of his street, because his watch needed a new battery. The door closed behind him, and the horns of the yellow buses dropped away. Inside, the air smelled of oil and old wood. Mr Okonkwo, a thin man with silver glasses, was sitting among hundreds of ticking clocks, and no two of them agreed. "Looking for something?" he asked, without looking up from the tiny wheel in his tweezers.

"A way to get more time," joked Chidi.

The tweezers stopped. Mr Okonkwo smiled strangely. From a dusty shelf, he took down a small brass clock and put it on the counter. It was heavier than it looked. Chidi looked closer and blinked. The face had thirteen numbers instead of twelve, all squeezed together.

"It is broken," Chidi said.

"Very likely," said Mr Okonkwo. "Take it. It is free."

Chidi hesitated. Nothing in Lagos was free. "Why?" he asked.

"Because the last person brought it back." The old man looked up at last, over his glasses. "Be careful. Time is not as simple as it looks."

Chidi laughed, paid for his battery and walked out into the noise with the clock in his bag. He was halfway home before he noticed its ticking. It was slightly out of step with his watch, as if an extra beat were hiding inside it.

questions.prompt: In which city does Chidi live?
options: Accra
Lagos
Abuja
Ibadan
questions.why: The text says his school day in Lagos began at seven. His father drives to Ibadan.

questions.prompt: Why was Chidi always behind by bedtime?
options: He slept all afternoon and did not begin his homework until late
His parents kept him away from school for three days each week
School, football, homework, chores and Ngozi filled up his whole day
He spent most of his evenings at the repair shop on his street
questions.why: His day ran from school at seven and football until five, and then came homework, chores and helping Ngozi.

questions.prompt: What does "as if she were telling it a secret" suggest about Ngozi's playing?
options: It is shy and almost impossible to hear
It is very loud and rather careless
It is quick and full of mistakes
It is gentle and full of feeling
questions.why: Telling someone a secret is quiet and close. The comparison makes her playing sound tender and personal.

questions.prompt: Why did Chidi go into the repair shop?
options: His watch needed a new battery
He had come to look for more time
He wanted to buy a clock for Ngozi
His violin needed a new string
questions.why: He went into the repair shop because his watch needed a new battery. His remark about more time was a joke.

questions.prompt: What was strange about the brass clock?
options: Its face had thirteen numbers
It was made of solid gold
It ran backwards all day
It had no hands at all
questions.why: The face had thirteen numbers instead of twelve, all squeezed together.

questions.prompt: What does Mr Okonkwo's reaction to Chidi's joke suggest?
options: He thinks the boy has been very rude to him
He has not heard what the boy said to him
He is too busy to give any attention to customers
He takes the idea of getting more time quite seriously
questions.why: The tweezers stop and he smiles strangely. Then he brings out the clock, as if the joke were a real request.

questions.prompt: Why might "the last person brought it back" worry a careful reader?
options: It suggests that the clock was too heavy for most people
It suggests that the shop only ever sells broken clocks
It suggests that the clock caused some kind of trouble
It suggests that the clock had been stolen from someone
questions.why: People do not usually return a free gift unless something is wrong with it, and straight after this he says, "Be careful."

questions.prompt: What did Chidi notice on the way home?
options: His new battery had already started running down
The clock's ticking was out of step with his watch
The yellow buses had all gone quiet on his street
The clock had stopped ticking as soon as he left
questions.why: It was slightly out of step with his watch, as if an extra beat were hiding inside it.

chapters.title: The Extra Hour
chapters.text:
That night, Chidi put the clock on his shelf, between his football boots and his geography book, and tried to sleep. Lagos was never quiet. A generator hummed next door, and somewhere a dog was barking at nothing. At exactly midnight, the clock began to chime: one, two, three, all the way to twelve. Chidi groaned and pulled the pillow over his head.

Then, after a small pause, it chimed once more.

At the thirteenth chime, the whole world stopped. The generator stopped. The dog stopped. The ceiling fan hung still in mid-spin. A moth froze in the air near the window with its wings spread. Outside, a car stood silent on the road with its headlights shining, and the night watchman across the street was halfway through a yawn.

Chidi crept to the window. Nothing moved. He looked in at Ngozi, who lay with one arm flung out, and he could not see her breathing. For a moment, he was very afraid. He was the only one awake in a world of statues. He touched the moth with one finger, and it stayed where it was, like a bead on an invisible string. In his room, the brass clock went on ticking, very slowly.

"Whoa," he whispered. "An extra hour!"

He used it well. He finished his maths homework at the desk with nobody calling his name. He went down to the yard and practised passing the football against the wall, and the thud did not wake a soul. He read half a book, just for pleasure, which he had not done since last term. He sharpened all his pencils, just because he could. On his way back in from the yard, he said good evening to the watchman across the street, and it felt very strange to get no answer. But the whole hour felt like the first deep breath he had taken in months.

When the hour was over, the clock ticked once, and the world started again. The fan turned. The watchman finished his yawn. The moth flew on.

Chidi got back into bed. He was not even tired. He fell asleep smiling, and he did not hear Ngozi sigh and turn over in the next room.

questions.prompt: What happened at the thirteenth chime?
options: The clock broke into pieces
All the lights went out
A storm began outside
The whole world stopped
questions.why: At the thirteenth chime, the whole world stopped.

questions.prompt: Which detail best shows that time itself had stopped?
options: The night watchman was frozen halfway through a yawn
A generator had been humming in the house next door
Chidi had pulled the pillow right over his head
The clock had chimed all the way up to twelve
questions.why: Nobody can stay halfway through a yawn. A sleeping street can be quiet, but a yawn stopped in the middle only happens if time has stopped.

questions.prompt: Why was Chidi very afraid for a moment?
options: The ticking clock had started to grow very much louder
Ngozi did not seem to be breathing, and he seemed to be alone
The moth had flown straight into his face in the dark
A stranger had come into the room and spoken to him
questions.why: He looked at Ngozi and could not see her breathing, and he was the only one awake in a world of statues.

questions.prompt: What did Chidi do with the extra hour?
options: He woke Ngozi and showed her the frozen moth
He walked to the repair shop and spoke to the owner
He did his maths, practised football and read
He slept for longer, then played a video game
questions.why: He finished his maths homework, practised passing the football against the wall, and read half a book.

questions.prompt: How could Chidi kick a football against a wall at midnight without trouble?
options: Nobody could hear it, because the world had stopped
The whole street was away visiting family in Ibadan
He wrapped the ball in an old towel to muffle it
The generator next door was making too much noise
questions.why: The text says the thud did not wake a soul. Everyone was frozen, so nobody could be disturbed.

questions.prompt: What does "the first deep breath he had taken in months" tell us?
options: He had been ill with a bad cough for several months
He had felt rushed and under pressure for a long time
He had been running too much at football practice
He had not been outside in the fresh air for months
questions.why: It is not about real breathing. After months of being behind, an hour with no pressure feels like relief.

questions.prompt: How did the extra hour end?
options: Ngozi woke and called out for her big brother
Chidi turned the clock's hands back to twelve
The moth flew into the fan and made a noise
The clock ticked once, and the world started again
questions.why: When the hour was over, the clock ticked once, and the world started again.

questions.prompt: Why might the writer mention Ngozi sighing at the end of the chapter?
options: To remind us that she is younger than her brother Chidi
To explain that she is a noisy sleeper who keeps Chidi awake
To hint that the extra hour may be having some effect on her
To show that she has been woken up by the noise of the ball
questions.why: The chapter ends on this small detail, just as Chidi is pleased and not even tired. It makes the reader wonder about her.

chapters.title: Too Good to Stop
chapters.text:
For a week, the clock chimed thirteen every midnight. Chidi's life changed. He finished his homework early, his football improved, and his teacher praised his neat work. The red ink vanished from his diary. His coach moved him up to the first team. He even had time to play cards with his friends in the evening, and he began to feel a little sorry for people who only had twenty-four hours. His mother looked at his marks and said, "Who are you, and what have you done with my son?"

"How do you do it?" asked his best friend, Emeka, at the bus stop. They had shared every secret since they were six.

"Just good planning," Chidi lied. It came out very easily, and that surprised him a little.

By the fifth night, the hour was not for homework any more. He put his feet on the desk and read comics, because he told himself he had earned it.

But he began to notice something odd. Ngozi was always tired now. At breakfast she yawned over her porridge, and during violin practice her bow slid off the strings. Her teacher sent a note home. The school concert was on Saturday week, and Ngozi had the solo. She had talked of nothing else for months, and now she hardly mentioned it.

"I do not know what is wrong," she said sadly. "I sleep all night, but I wake up exhausted."

Their mother felt her forehead and took her temperature, and there was nothing wrong. "She is growing," she said. But she did not look sure, and she stood looking at Ngozi for a long time.

Chidi felt a tiny cold feeling in his stomach. He thought about the clock. A whole extra hour, every night. Where did it come from? He had taken care never to ask that question. He remembered the old man's eyes over the silver glasses, and the words, the last person brought it back.

Then he pushed the thought away. After all, it could not possibly be connected.

That night, he lay awake and waited for midnight anyway. At the thirteenth chime, he looked for a moment towards Ngozi's door. Then he reached for his comic.

questions.prompt: For how long did the clock chime thirteen every midnight?
options: For a single night
For a week
For a whole month
For a whole year
questions.why: The chapter opens with "For a week, the clock chimed thirteen every midnight."

questions.prompt: What changed for Chidi at school?
options: His marks fell, and his teacher sent a note home
He gave up football and stayed home in the evening
His work was on time, and his teacher praised it
He moved to a new class with his friend Emeka
questions.why: He finished his homework early, his teacher praised his neat work, and the red ink vanished from his diary.

questions.prompt: Why did the easy lie surprise Chidi a little?
options: He was not used to hiding things from his best friend
He had already told Emeka all about the brass clock
He had not thought that Emeka would ever ask him
He did not know the meaning of the word planning
questions.why: They had shared every secret since they were six, so lying to Emeka was new for him.

questions.prompt: How did Chidi's use of the hour change by the fifth night?
options: He stayed in bed asleep the whole time
He gave it to his friends for playing cards
He began to spend it helping his sister
He stopped working and read comics in it
questions.why: By the fifth night, the hour was not for homework any more. He put his feet on the desk and read comics.

questions.prompt: Why was Ngozi's tiredness such a serious problem just now?
options: She had the solo at the school concert very soon
Her teacher was going to move away from Lagos
She had a very important maths test the next week
Her mother had just lost her job at the hospital
questions.why: The school concert was on Saturday week, and Ngozi had the solo.

questions.prompt: What did their mother do when she was worried about Ngozi?
options: She looked through Chidi's room to find the cause
She felt her forehead and took her temperature
She kept her away from school for a whole week
She rang the violin teacher and asked for advice
questions.why: Their mother felt her forehead and took her temperature, and there was nothing wrong.

questions.prompt: What does "He had taken care never to ask that question" show?
options: He had asked Mr Okonkwo, and he had got no reply
He had forgotten all about it as soon as he got home
He did not understand how clocks and watches work
Part of him suspected the answer and did not want to know
questions.why: Taking care not to ask means he knew there was a question and avoided it on purpose.

questions.prompt: Does Chidi truly believe that "it could not possibly be connected"?
options: Yes, his mother has told him that she has found the cause
No, he has just proved that the clock is hurting his sister
No, he is telling himself that so that he can keep the hour
Yes, he has good evidence that Ngozi is simply growing
questions.why: He feels a cold fear and pushes the thought away, then looks towards her door before reaching for his comic. He is avoiding what he suspects.

chapters.title: The Clockmaker's Warning
chapters.text:
The next evening, Ngozi fell asleep in the middle of her violin practice. The bow slipped from her hand and rolled across the floor, and she did not wake. Chidi stood in the doorway and looked at her. She was eight years old, and there were grey shadows under her eyes. He carried her to bed, and she did not stir even when he took off her shoes.

Then he took the brass clock in his bag and ran down the street to the repair shop.

It was long past closing time, but the door stood open. Mr Okonkwo was waiting there, as if he had expected him. Two cups of tea were on the counter, and both of them were already poured.

"I wondered when you would come," he said. "You have noticed, then."

"Noticed what?" Chidi's voice shook. He put the clock on the counter, and all the clocks in the shop seemed to tick more softly.

"The clock does not make time," said the old man. "It only moves it. Every extra hour you use is taken from somebody close to you. Somebody who loves you, and whom you love. They lose an hour of rest and do not know why."

Chidi felt his legs go weak. He sat down on a box of spare springs. Seven nights, one hour every night. He remembered the comics, and his feet on the desk. "Ngozi," he whispered. "I have been taking her hours."

"Yes."

"You knew!" Chidi was shouting now. He had never shouted at an adult in his life. "Why did you give it to me?"

Mr Okonkwo let him finish. Then he took off his glasses, and without them he looked very old. "I told you to be careful, and you laughed," he said. "Nobody believes a warning about time until they have spent some. When I was your age, I had a brother. Nobody warned me at all."

The shop was silent for a while, apart from the ticking.

"Then I will smash it," said Chidi.

"You may. But the hours would still be owed, and she would go on paying for them. And there is only one way to stop it," said Mr Okonkwo. "You must give back all the hours you have taken."

questions.prompt: What happened during Ngozi's violin practice?
options: She started to cry and said that she had a bad fever
She played her solo better than she had ever played it
She fell asleep, and the bow rolled across the floor
She broke a string and went to look for her brother
questions.why: Ngozi fell asleep in the middle of her violin practice. The bow slipped from her hand and rolled across the floor.

questions.prompt: Which detail suggests that Mr Okonkwo had been expecting Chidi?
options: His glasses were lying on the counter
There was a box of spare springs on the floor
There were hundreds of clocks in the shop
Two cups of tea had already been poured
questions.why: He was waiting at the open door after closing time, and two cups of tea were already poured, one of them clearly for a visitor.

questions.prompt: What does the clock really do?
options: It stops time for ever for everyone
It moves time from one person to another
It makes brand new time out of nothing
It tells the wrong time on purpose
questions.why: "The clock does not make time," said the old man. "It only moves it."

questions.prompt: From whom is each extra hour taken?
options: Somebody who loves the user, and whom the user loves
The person who last brought the clock to the shop
The clockmaker, who must lose an hour for every sale
A stranger living in another part of the same city
questions.why: Every extra hour is taken from somebody close to you. "Somebody who loves you, and whom you love."

questions.prompt: Why does Chidi remember the comics at this moment?
options: He wishes he had brought one along to the shop to read
He feels guilty that he spent his sister's rest on something so idle
He thinks that the comics are what made Ngozi so ill
He wants to give the comics to Mr Okonkwo in payment
questions.why: He has just learned that each hour came from someone he loves, and he recalls lying with his feet on the desk. The memory shames him.

questions.prompt: How does Mr Okonkwo answer the question "Why did you give it to me?"
options: He says that Chidi had stolen the clock and that it was never a gift at all
He says that he wanted Chidi's homework to improve and that it did improve
He says that the clock was broken and he did not know what it would do
He says he warned Chidi, and nobody believes such a warning until it costs them
questions.why: He says, "I told you to be careful, and you laughed. Nobody believes a warning about time until they have spent some."

questions.prompt: What do Mr Okonkwo's words about his brother suggest?
options: He learned how to mend clocks from his older brother
His brother lives in Ibadan and drives a delivery van
He once took hours from his own brother in the same way
His brother is the person who brought the clock back
questions.why: He says, "When I was your age, I had a brother. Nobody warned me at all." He looks very old as he says it, so he seems to have made the same mistake.

questions.prompt: Why would smashing the clock not solve the problem?
options: The hours would still be owed, and Ngozi would go on paying
Mr Okonkwo would have to be paid for the broken clock
The clock is made of brass and is too strong to smash
The shop would be full of the sound of chiming for days
questions.why: "You may. But the hours would still be owed, and she would go on paying for them."

chapters.title: Giving It Back
chapters.text:
"But how?" asked Chidi. "I cannot just hand her seven hours."

"You can spend your hours on her," said Mr Okonkwo. "Care is how time goes back, and no magic trick will do it. For every hour you borrowed, give an hour of your own time to Ngozi, and do it gladly. When you have repaid them all, the clock will stop." He looked at Chidi over his cup. "Gladly is the hard part. An hour given with a sour face counts for nothing."

Chidi took a deep breath and ran home. That night, he put the clock aside. Each midnight it still chimed thirteen, and each midnight he stayed in bed with his eyes shut and let the hour go by. For the next week he got up early.

The first hour went badly. He sat on the edge of Ngozi's bed with his arms folded while she played her scales. He listened to the sound of a football game out in the street. He knew that it did not count, even before she looked up and said, "You can go if you want."

So on Tuesday, he did it again, and this time he asked her to show him how to hold the bow. He was terrible. The noise he made sounded like a goat on a hot roof, and Ngozi laughed for the first time in days. Something in his chest came loose.

After that, it grew easier. He helped Ngozi with her scales. He carried her violin to school. He sat in the front row at her lessons and clapped louder than anyone, until her teacher politely asked him to stop clapping in the middle of a scale.

On Thursday, at the bus stop, he told Emeka the truth, or as much as he could. "It was never good planning," he said. "I was cheating, and someone else was paying for it." Emeka looked at him for a long moment. "Do you want help with the maths?" he asked.

Some days, his homework was late and football practice was missed. The red ink came back. It was not easy. But when Ngozi laughed again, Chidi found that he did not mind. The grey shadows faded from under her eyes, and by Friday she could play her whole solo without a slip.

questions.prompt: How many hours did Chidi owe?
options: Three
Five
Seven
Thirteen
questions.why: He says, "I cannot just hand her seven hours." He took one hour on each of seven nights.

questions.prompt: How must the hours be given back?
options: By letting Ngozi use the clock for a week
By winding the clock backwards seven times
By paying Mr Okonkwo for the time he used
By spending his own time on Ngozi gladly
questions.why: "For every hour you borrowed, give an hour of your own time to Ngozi, and do it gladly."

questions.prompt: Why did Chidi know that the first hour "did not count"?
options: The clock had chimed thirteen at the end of that same hour
He had given it with folded arms and his mind on the football
Mr Okonkwo had told him that he must begin on a Tuesday
Ngozi had played her scales badly and then gone to sleep
questions.why: Mr Okonkwo said an hour with a sour face counts for nothing. Chidi sat with his arms folded, listening to the football game.

questions.prompt: What made Ngozi laugh for the first time in days?
options: Chidi's terrible attempt to play the violin
A goat that had climbed onto a hot roof
Her teacher asking Chidi to stop clapping
A joke told by Emeka at the bus stop
questions.why: He asked her to show him how to hold the bow. He was terrible, and the noise made Ngozi laugh.

questions.prompt: What does "Something in his chest came loose" suggest?
options: He had hurt himself while holding the bow
He felt his guilt and worry begin to ease
He was having trouble breathing in the heat
He had a bad cold that was getting better
questions.why: It comes straight after she laughs for the first time in days. It describes a feeling of relief, and it is not about an injury.

questions.prompt: How has Chidi changed since he told Emeka "Just good planning"?
options: He now tells the truth, even though it makes him look bad
He now thinks that planning is the only way to succeed
He now refuses to speak to Emeka at the bus stop
He now tells many more lies to keep his friends
questions.why: In chapter three he lied easily. Now he says, "I was cheating, and someone else was paying for it."

questions.prompt: What does Emeka's reply show about him?
options: He has not heard what Chidi has just told him
He wants Chidi to do his maths homework for him
He is too angry to talk about what has happened
He is a loyal friend who offers help without judging
questions.why: Chidi admits to cheating, and Emeka simply offers help with the maths. He does not scold him or walk away.

questions.prompt: What did helping Ngozi cost Chidi?
options: A week away from school and from home
The loss of all his comics and his watch
Late homework and missed football practice
A broken clock and an angry clockmaker
questions.why: Some days, his homework was late and football practice was missed. The red ink came back.

chapters.title: Twelve Is Enough
chapters.text:
On Saturday evening, Ngozi played at the school concert. Their mother had swapped a shift, and their father came straight from Ibadan with dust on his shoes. Ngozi walked out in her white dress, very small beside the piano, and she tucked the violin under her chin.

Her bow danced over the strings, and the hall was silent until the last note. Even the babies stopped crying. When she finished, the audience stood up and cheered. In the front row, Chidi clapped until his hands hurt. She looked straight at him and crossed her eyes for half a second, the way she did at home. He laughed out loud and had to pretend it was a cough.

That night at midnight, the clock chimed twelve times. Only twelve. Chidi lay in the dark and held his breath, waiting for the next chime. It did not come. The ceiling fan went on turning, and the dog went on barking. Nothing stopped, and the moth outside kept on flying. Chidi smiled in the dark. He had never been so pleased to lose an hour.

The next morning, he took the clock back to Mr Okonkwo. It looked smaller somehow. The old man was bent over a tiny wheel, and he did not seem surprised.

"Keep it, if you like," he said. "It will remind you. Time is the only thing that we all have in equal amounts."

"I think I understand," said Chidi. "I never needed more hours. I needed to use the ones I had."

Mr Okonkwo looked up and smiled, an ordinary smile this time. Chidi looked at the clock for a moment. Then he put it on the counter and pushed it across.

"Someone else will come in looking for more time," said the old man. "Someone always does."

"Then I think," said Chidi, "that you should put a sign on it."

Mr Okonkwo began to laugh. It sounded rusty, as if he did not do it very often, and the laugh followed Chidi out into the noise of the street.

On the way home, he wrote a timetable on the back of his hand: homework, football, Ngozi. It was not very neat, and there would still be late days. Then he looked at the sky and decided that twelve numbers were plenty.

questions.prompt: Who came to watch Ngozi's concert?
options: Both of their parents, and Chidi
Only Mr Okonkwo and his brother
Nobody from her family at all
Only her teacher and Emeka
questions.why: Their mother had swapped a shift, their father came straight from Ibadan, and Chidi sat in the front row.

questions.prompt: How did the audience react to the solo?
options: They left before the last note
They asked her to play it again
They stood up and cheered
They talked among themselves
questions.why: When she finished, the audience stood up and cheered.

questions.prompt: Why did Ngozi cross her eyes at Chidi?
options: She had made a mistake and wanted to hide it from him
The bright lights in the hall had made her feel very dizzy
She was cross with him for clapping far too loudly
It was a private family joke, and it showed she was herself again
questions.why: The text says she did it the way she did at home. A child who is exhausted would hardly play a joke, so she has recovered.

questions.prompt: How many times did the clock chime that midnight?
options: Eleven
Twelve
Thirteen
Fourteen
questions.why: That night at midnight, the clock chimed twelve times. Only twelve.

questions.prompt: What does "He had never been so pleased to lose an hour" mean?
options: He had lost his watch at the concert and did not care about it
He was glad that the debt was paid and the extra hour had gone
He was happy that he could stay in bed for longer the next day
He had been hoping that the concert would finish an hour early
questions.why: Twelve chimes mean the clock has stopped its magic, as Mr Okonkwo said it would once the hours were repaid.

questions.prompt: What does Mr Okonkwo say about time?
options: It belongs to whoever owns the most clocks
It is the only thing that money can always buy
It is the only thing we all have in equal amounts
It moves faster in Lagos than it does elsewhere
questions.why: He says, "Time is the only thing that we all have in equal amounts."

questions.prompt: Why does Chidi say the clock should have a sign on it?
options: To stop Mr Okonkwo from losing it among the other clocks
To show customers the time in other parts of the world
To tell people the correct price of the brass clock
To warn the next person before they make the same mistake
questions.why: Mr Okonkwo says someone else will come looking for more time. Chidi has learned that a warning needs to be clear.

questions.prompt: What lesson did Chidi learn?
options: He needed to use the hours he had, and he did not need more
He needed a better clock to help him with his homework
He needed to keep away from every kind of magic for ever
He needed to stop playing football and looking after Ngozi
questions.why: He says, "I never needed more hours. I needed to use the ones I had."
